catalog_quote: [Eades 1976:25, as carried by StressTyp2] Most words have initial main stress. Some words have primary stress on the second syllable; most of these words have a long vowel in the second syllable. There is no secondary stress.. Dharrawal, from archival transcriptions] Stress falls on the first syllable in disyllabic words and no example is found in the source material that shows stress on the final syllable in a disyllabic word.. In words with three syllables or more, primary stress falls on the first or second syllable. Where stress is marked on a second syllable in a polysyllabic word, a long vowel in that stressed syllable is in some cases indicated.. It is possible that collectors may have misinterpreted long vowel pronunciation as stress on that syllable.. But Mathews also transcribed words tha…

audit.reasoning: The classification (weight-hedged: initial default, some peninitial stress mostly on long vowels, no secondary stress) rests on Eades 1976:25-26, the sole audio-based sketch of this no-longer-spoken language, but we hold only StressTyp2's carry of that passage, confirmed verbatim in the held bundle (passage 878). The supporting Besold 2012 PhD (pp.113-114) is held and its quoted sentences are confirmed verbatim; it independently agrees (initial stress; second-syllable stress in polysyllables sometimes with a marked long vowel; length and stress independent in some Mathews forms), so nothing suggests the hedged coding is wrong. Glottolog's four descriptive refs contain nothing better; Mathews 1901 (downloaded now, public domain) has no stress statement. No instrumental or modern phonology study exists. The one gap is direct sight of Eades pp.25-26 (in copyright; archive.org lending / print o
audit.second_reader_evidence: Quote finding re-checked and confirmed as the compilers states. (a) Eades 1976:25 is held only as StressTyp2's carried passage: passage 878, pages '25', text character-identical to the record's Eades segment ('Most words have initial main stress. Some words have primary stress on the second syllable; most of these words have a long vowel in the second syllable. There is no secondary stress.'); the ST1 remark ('Not all words that have stress on the second syllable have a long vowel there. This may be a consequence of a vowel-reduction process (Eades 1976:26)') is a database paraphrase, also in the bundle notes. is archive.org

sources.note: Silent on stress. The catalog record for Dharawal (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so nothing to agree with or contradict. Context only (not the listed work): in the same volume, Reid's ch. 25 'English influence on the pronunciation of re-awakened Aboriginal languages' (p. 327-328 of the PDF) makes a general NSW-wide remark that 'stress on either the first syllable of a word or on long vowels were the most common patterns', illustrated with Gamilaraay, not Dharawal; it is not a Dharawal-specific statement and is not entered as a reading here.

sources.citation: Mathews, R. H. (1901). The Thurrawal language. Journal and Proceedings of the Royal Society of New South Wales 35: 127-160.
sources.quote: None. The Orthography section describes letters and sounds only; no statement on accent/stress anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent|stress|emphas = 0 hits). Mathews' stress marks exist only as apostrophes in his word transcriptions, which is what Besold 2012 analyses.

sources.note: Full text of the pronunciation section read: gives an English-based practical orthography and 'The Dharawal Alphabet' with example words; the only prosodic statement is about word emphasis (stress): 'Normally, the emphasis occurs on the second syllable of a word', with apostrophes marking emphasised syllables in long compound forms (example Galumban'winima'kamawi'dyawa, emphasis on loom, wi, ka, dya); no lexical or grammatical tone is described; the one-page introduction mentions 'vocal tone' only as expressive voice quality ('given colour by.. the tone of our voices'), not as a phonological…

tone.quote: Oftentimes I have used the apostrophe to indicate where the emphases should be on words. Normally, the emphasis occurs on the second syllable of a word, however in many cases the words are actually comprised of a number of words and I have used the apostrophe to denote the emphasised sounds.
